source_text: Temptabis ad haec de nomine dei concutere retractatum ; ut passiuo et in alios quoque permisso, quia scriptum sit: ! deus deorum stetit in ecclesia deorum, in medio autem deos diiudicabit, et: ego dixi, uos dii estis. nec tamen idcirco eis competat possessio summi magni, quia dii cognominentur; ita nec creatori. respondebo et stulto, qui nec hoc recogitauerit, ne tantundem et in deum Marcionis possit retorqueri, ut et illum deum dictum nec ideo tamen summum magnum probatum, sicut nec angeli aut homines creatoris. si communio nominum condicionibus praeiudicat, quanti nequam serui regum nominibus insultant, Alexandri et Darii et Olofernae? nec tamen ideo regibus id quod sunt detrahetur. nam et ipsa idola gentium dei uulgo, sed deus nemo ea re, qua deus dicitur. ita ego non nomini dei nec sono nec notae nominis huius summum magnum in creatore defendo, sed ipsi substantiae, cui nomen hoc contigit. hanc inueniens solam innatam infectam, solam aeternam et uniuersitatis conditricem, non nomini, sed statui, nec appellationi, sed condicioni eius summum magnum et adscribo et uindico. et ideo. quia deus iam uocari obtinuit substantia cui adscribo, nomini me adscribere putas, quia necesse est per nomen ostendam cui adscribam substantiae, scilicet qua constat qui deus dicitur. at summum magnum ex substantia, non ex nomine, deputatur. denique hoc et Marcion suo deo uindicans, secundum statum, non secundum uocabulum uindicat. id ergo summum magnum, quod deo adscribimus ex substantiae lege, non ex nominis sorte, contendimus ex pari esse debere in duobus, qui ea substantia constant, quae deus dicitur, quia in quantum dii uocantur, id est summa magna, substantiae scilicet mento innatae et aeternae ac per hoc magnae et summae, in tantum non possit summum magnum minus et deterius alio summo magno haberi. si summi magni felicitas et sublimitas et integritas stabit in deo Marcionis, stabit aeque et in nostro, si non et in nostro, aeque nec in Marcionis. ergo nec paria erunt duo summa magna, quia prohibet disposita iam regula summi magni comparationem non sustinens, nec disparia, quia et alia summi magni regula occurrit, diminutionem non admittens. haesisti, Marcion, in medio Ponti tui aestu. utrimque te fluctus ueritatis inuoluunt. nec pares nec dispares deos sistere potes. duo enim non sunt. quod pertineat proprie ad numeri retractatum, quamquam tota materia de duobus deis dimicetur, his interim lineis eum clusimus, intra quas de singularibus iam proprietatibus congrediemur.
thought_title: Challenge to Marcion's View of God
pass_a_gloss: You will try to shake by these things the retracted name of God, so that, with the passive and also permitted to others, because it is written: God of gods stood in the church of gods, and in the middle, however, he will judge gods, and: I said, you are gods. And yet, therefore, the possession of the highest great one does not belong to them, because they are called gods; thus, neither to the Creator. I will respond also to the foolish one, who has not considered this, lest it be possible to retort the same also against the God of Marcion, so that he also is called God, but not therefore proven to be the highest great one, just as neither the angels nor the men of the Creator. If the sharing of names prejudges conditions, how many wicked slaves insult with the names of kings, of Alexander and Darius and Holofernes? And yet, therefore, what they are is not taken away from the kings. For also the idols of the gentiles are commonly called gods, but no one is God by that by which he is called God. Thus, I do not defend the highest great one in the Creator by the name of God, nor by the sound, nor by the mark of this name, but by the substance itself, to which this name belongs. Finding this alone to be innate, uncorrupted, alone eternal, and the creator of the universe, I ascribe and vindicate the highest great one not to the name, but to the state, not to the appellation, but to the condition. And therefore, because the substance to which I ascribe already obtains the name of God, you think that I ascribe to the name, because it is necessary to show by the name to which substance I ascribe, namely, by which it is consistent that he is called God. But the highest great one is reckoned from the substance, not from the name. Finally, Marcion also, vindicating his God, vindicates according to the state, not according to the word. Therefore, we contend that the highest great one, which we ascribe to God from the law of substance, not from the lot of the name, ought to be equal in the two who consist of that substance which is called God, because insofar as they are called gods, that is, the highest great ones, namely, the substance innate and eternal, and therefore great and highest, to that extent it is not possible for one highest great one to be less and worse than another highest great one. If the happiness and sublimity and integrity of the highest great one stand in the God of Marcion, they will stand equally in ours; if not also in ours, then equally not in Marcion's. Therefore, the two highest great ones will not be equal, because the already established rule of the highest great one does not sustain comparison, nor unequal, because another rule of the highest great one occurs, not admitting diminution. You have hesitated, Marcion, in the middle of your Pontus of turmoil. The waves of truth envelop you on both sides. You are not able to establish equal or unequal gods. For there are not two. What pertains properly to the retracted number, although the whole matter is fought about two gods, we have enclosed him within these lines, within which we will now contend about the singular properties.

bible_refs.note: God of gods stood in the church of gods

pass_b_english: You will try to shake the retracted name of God with these arguments; the move is passive, and you allow others to use it too, because Scripture says: "God takes his stand in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment" (Ps 82:1), and again: "I said, 'You are gods'" (Ps 82:6). Yet that does not grant them possession of the Supreme Great One simply because they bear the title "gods"; the same holds for the Creator.

I will answer the fool who has not considered this, lest the same retort be turned against Marcion's God: that he too is called God, yet not thereby proven to be the Supreme Great One, any more than the Creator's angels or humans. If the sharing of names prejudges natures, how many wicked slaves insult kings by usurping the names of Alexander, Darius, and Holofernes? Yet the kings lose nothing of what they are. The nations' idols are commonly called gods, but no one is God by the very fact of being so called.

Therefore I do not defend the Supreme Great One in the Creator by the name of God, nor by its sound, nor by the mere label of this name, but by the substance itself to which this name belongs. Finding that substance alone innate, uncorrupted, alone eternal, and the maker of the universe, I ascribe and vindicate the Supreme Great One not to the name but to the reality, not to the appellation but to the condition.

And because the substance to which I ascribe it already bears the name God, you think I ascribe it to the name, since I must use the name to indicate which substance I mean—namely, the one by which it is consistent that he is called God. But the Supreme Great One is reckoned from the substance, not from the name. Even Marcion, vindicating his God, vindicates according to the reality, not the word.

So we contend that the Supreme Great One, which we ascribe to God from the law of substance, not from the lottery of the name, must be equal in the two who consist of that substance which is called God. Insofar as they are called gods—that is, Supreme Great Ones, the substance innate and eternal, and therefore great and supreme—to that extent one Supreme Great One cannot be less and worse than another.

If the happiness, sublimity, and integrity of the Supreme Great One stand in Marcion's God, they will stand equally in ours; if not in ours either, then equally not in Marcion's. Therefore the two Supreme Great Ones will not be equal, because the already established rule of the Supreme Great One does not sustain comparison, nor unequal, because another rule of the Supreme Great One arises, not admitting diminution.

You have stalled, Marcion, in the middle of your Pontic storm. The waves of truth envelop you on both sides. You cannot establish gods as equal or unequal, for there are not two. What pertains properly to the retracted number—although the whole dispute is fought over two gods—we have enclosed him within these lines, within which we will now engage on the singular properties.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological argument regarding substance (substantia) versus name (nomen). Pass B correctly identifies and expands the scripture citations (Psalm 82:1 and 82:6) which were alluded to in the Latin. The distinction between 'state/reality' (statum) and 'appellation/word' (uocabulum) is maintained. All clauses in the Latin are accounted for in both Pass A and B.
